scope: A-level-only Organic Chemistry sections 3.3.7–3.3.16, including all 19 numbered subsections; each row is an evidence-backed selected learning demand, not a claim of full exhaustive specification certification.
keyFindings: Mechanism pieces and reactions are often already memorised; drawn complete electron-arrow mechanisms remain less frequently evidenced.
Chiral 3D drawing, benzene thermochemistry, polymer repeat units, amino-acid peptides, up-to-four-step synthesis, combined spectroscopy and RP12 interpretation need original assessed application.
New A2 content must not be placed in a Year 1 mock-only filter merely because it appears in the full specification.
Some older automated NMR n+1 questions extend beyond AQA's named doublet/triplet/quartet requirement, so the scope should be labelled enrichment rather than deleted.

rows.requirement: Recognise a single chiral centre bonded to four different groups

cards.front: What is a chiral centre?
cards.back: Usually a carbon bonded to four different groups.

questions.prompt: Determine whether CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃ can exhibit optical isomerism. Identify the chiral carbon and name the four different groups attached.
markPoints: Carbon 2 is chiral.
Groups: H, OH, CH₃ and CH₂CH₃.
Two enantiomers are possible.

rows.requirement: State that enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images

cards.front: What is an enantiomer?
cards.back: One of two non-superimposable mirror-image stereoisomers.

rows.requirement: Explain why enantiomers rotate plane-polarised light differently

cards.front: What causes optical isomerism?
cards.back: A chiral carbon bonded to four different groups gives non-superimposable mirror-image enantiomers.

rows.requirement: Define an equal-mole racemic mixture

cards.front: Define a racemic mixture.
cards.back: Equal amounts of the two enantiomers.

questions.prompt: A mixture contains equal amounts of two enantiomers. Explain why its overall rotation of plane-polarised light is zero.
markPoints: Each enantiomer rotates the plane by equal magnitude.
The rotations are in opposite directions.
In a 50:50 racemate they cancel.

rows.requirement: Explain optical inactivity of a racemate

cards.front: Why does a racemic mixture give no net optical rotation?
cards.back: The enantiomers' rotations cancel.

questions.prompt: A mixture contains equal amounts of two enantiomers. Explain why its overall rotation of plane-polarised light is zero.
markPoints: Each enantiomer rotates the plane by equal magnitude.
The rotations are in opposite directions.
In a 50:50 racemate they cancel.

rows.requirement: Identify an asymmetric centre in an unfamiliar 2D formula

cards.front: What is a chiral carbon atom in basic A-level organic chemistry?
cards.back: A tetrahedral carbon bonded to four different groups.

questions.prompt: Determine whether CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃ can exhibit optical isomerism. Identify the chiral carbon and name the four different groups attached.
markPoints: Carbon 2 is chiral.
Groups: H, OH, CH₃ and CH₂CH₃.
Two enantiomers are possible.

rows.requirement: Draw a correctly oriented 3D enantiomer pair from one chiral carbon

cards.front: What is a chiral centre?
cards.back: Usually a carbon bonded to four different groups.

rows.limitation: Existing questions discuss chirality; no directly evidenced unfamiliar pair-drawing task.

rows.requirement: Explain why interaction with a chiral biological site may differ

questions.prompt: Why can two enantiomers have almost identical bulk physical properties yet interact differently with biological receptors?
markPoints: They are mirror-image stereoisomers.
Ordinary achiral properties are alike.
Many receptors are chiral and have stereospecific binding sites.

rows.requirement: Identify polarity of C=O and nucleophilic attack at its carbon

cards.front: Why are carbonyl compounds attacked at carbon?
cards.back: Their C=O bond is polar, with carbon δ+.

rows.requirement: Distinguish aldehydes from ketones using Tollens and Fehling observations

cards.front: What observation shows a positive Tollens' test?
cards.back: Silver mirror or grey silver deposit.

cards.front: What observation shows a positive Fehling's test?
cards.back: Brick-red precipitate.

questions.prompt: An unknown carbonyl compound gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent. State what functional group is indicated and why a ketone does not usually give this observation.
markPoints: Tollens' reagent gives a silver mirror with an aldehyde.
The aldehyde is oxidised to a carboxylate/carboxylic acid derivative.
Ordinary ketones are not readily oxidised in this test.

rows.requirement: Identify oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid

cards.front: What is the oxidation product of an aldehyde?
cards.back: A carboxylic acid.

rows.requirement: Identify alcohol classes formed by aldehyde versus ketone reduction

cards.front: What organic class comes from aldehyde reduction?
cards.back: A primary alcohol.

cards.front: What organic class comes from ketone reduction?
cards.back: A secondary alcohol.

questions.prompt: Propanone is reduced by NaBH₄. Explain why propan-2-ol is formed rather than propan-1-ol.
markPoints: The carbonyl carbon in propanone is carbon 2.
Nucleophilic hydride addition changes C=O into C–OH at carbon 2.
The carbon skeleton stays unchanged.

rows.requirement: Explain hydride as the nucleophile in NaBH4 nucleophilic addition

cards.front: What reagent reduces aldehydes and ketones?
cards.back: NaBH₄, sodium tetrahydridoborate.

questions.prompt: Propanal reacts with NaBH₄ followed by acidic work-up. Name the product and explain the role of the hydride ion.
markPoints: Product is propan-1-ol.
Hydride H⁻ is a nucleophile that attacks the carbonyl carbon.
The alkoxide is protonated to form alcohol.

rows.requirement: Draw both stages of carbonyl reduction with H- and electron-pair arrows

cards.front: Where do carbonyl π electrons go in nucleophilic addition?
cards.back: Toward oxygen while a new bond to carbon forms.

rows.limitation: The class and arrow location are in cards but no full unfamiliar carbonyl-reduction drawing is directly evidenced.

rows.requirement: Write reduction equations using [H] and correct product structures

cards.front: What forms when a ketone is reduced?
cards.back: A secondary alcohol.

cards.front: What forms when an aldehyde is reduced?
cards.back: A primary alcohol.

rows.limitation: Product classes recalled, but direct equation-writing application is not clearly tested.

rows.requirement: Recall the hydroxynitrile structure formed by carbonyl addition

cards.front: What groups are attached to the same carbon in a hydroxynitrile?
cards.back: A hydroxyl group and a nitrile group.

rows.requirement: Outline the nucleophilic addition electron-pair movement in hydroxynitrile formation

cards.front: What mechanism occurs when HCN adds to a carbonyl compound?
cards.back: Nucleophilic addition.

cards.front: Where do carbonyl π electrons go in nucleophilic addition?
cards.back: Toward oxygen while a new bond to carbon forms.

rows.limitation: Separate arrow-location recall exists; a complete drawn mechanism is not shown in the mapped main-bank questions.

rows.requirement: Explain why a planar carbonyl may form an enantiomer mixture

cards.front: Why can nucleophilic addition to a planar carbonyl produce enantiomers?
cards.back: The nucleophile can approach from either face.

rows.requirement: Recognise that cyanide-containing compounds have significant toxicity hazards
rows.limitation: Safety recognition should be limited to a short hazard-awareness fact without procedures or access details.

rows.requirement: Identify weak acidity and reaction with carbonate

cards.front: Why is a carboxylic acid described as weak?
cards.back: Only a fraction of its molecules dissociate into ions in water.

cards.front: Why do carboxylic acids react with carbonates?
cards.back: Their acidic protons react with carbonate ions, releasing carbon dioxide.

questions.prompt: Ethanoic acid reacts with aqueous sodium carbonate. Write the balanced equation and name the gas.
markPoints: 2CH₃COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂.
The gas is carbon dioxide.

rows.requirement: State ester functional-group structure and naming convention

cards.front: What is the ester functional group?
How do you name an ester?
cards.back: Alkyl name from the alcohol first, then the acid-derived –oate name.

rows.requirement: Explain reversible carboxylic-acid and alcohol esterification

cards.front: What is the general equation for esterification?
cards.back: Carboxylic acid + alcohol ⇌ ester + water.

questions.prompt: Write the reversible reaction of propanoic acid with ethanol. Name the ester produced.
markPoints: CH₃CH₂COOH + CH₃CH₂OH ⇌ CH₃CH₂COOCH₂CH₃ + H₂O.
The ester is ethyl propanoate.

rows.requirement: Recall common uses of esters

cards.front: Give four typical applications of esters.
cards.back: Solvents, plasticisers, perfume ingredients and food flavourings.

rows.requirement: Identify fats and oils as glycerol triesters

cards.front: What is glycerol's systematic name?
cards.back: Propane-1,2,3-triol.

cards.front: What are fats and vegetable oils made from chemically?
cards.back: Triglycerides containing three ester links to glycerol.

rows.requirement: Distinguish acidic ester hydrolysis from alkaline ester hydrolysis products

cards.front: What is produced by acidic ester hydrolysis?
cards.back: A carboxylic acid and an alcohol.

cards.front: What is produced by alkaline ester hydrolysis?
cards.back: A carboxylate salt and an alcohol.

rows.requirement: Recognise triglyceride hydrolysis as producing soap and glycerol

cards.front: What is saponification?
cards.back: Alkaline hydrolysis of fats or oils.

cards.front: What are the main products of triglyceride saponification?
cards.back: Soap (long-chain carboxylate salts) and glycerol.

rows.requirement: Define biodiesel as fatty-acid methyl esters

cards.front: What type of substances make up biodiesel?
cards.back: Methyl esters of long-chain carboxylic acids.

rows.requirement: Distinguish transesterification from ordinary hydrolysis

cards.front: What does transesterification mean?
cards.back: Exchange of the alcohol-derived part of an ester.

cards.front: How is transesterification different from hydrolysis?
cards.back: Transesterification exchanges an ester group; hydrolysis breaks an ester bond.

rows.requirement: Interpret unfamiliar triglyceride structures and product stoichiometry

cards.front: What is the stoichiometric number of fatty acid methyl esters per triglyceride?
cards.back: Three methyl ester molecules correspond to one triglyceride.

rows.limitation: Stoichiometry recall exists but independently drawing a glycerol triester or identifying individual ester linkages is not mapped.

rows.requirement: Recognise acyl chlorides, acid anhydrides and amide groups

cards.front: What is the general formula of an acyl chloride?
cards.back: R–C(=O)–Cl.

cards.front: What group links the two carbonyls in an acid anhydride?
cards.back: A bridging oxygen: RCO–O–COR′.

cards.front: What is an amide functional group?
cards.back: A carbonyl directly bonded to nitrogen, e.g. –CONH₂.

rows.requirement: Recall products of acyl chloride reaction with water or alcohol

cards.front: What is the organic product class of acyl chloride hydrolysis?
cards.back: A carboxylic acid.

cards.front: What is the organic product class of alcohol acylation?
cards.back: An ester.

questions.prompt: Write the reaction of ethanoyl chloride with water and name the organic product.
markPoints: CH₃COCl + H₂O → CH₃COOH + HCl.
Organic product is ethanoic acid.

rows.requirement: Recall amide products from ammonia and primary amines

cards.front: What is the organic product class when ammonia is acylated?
cards.back: A primary amide, RCONH₂.

cards.front: What is the organic product class when a primary amine is acylated?
cards.back: An N-substituted amide, RCONHR′.

questions.prompt: Ethanoyl chloride reacts with excess methylamine. Give the name of the organic product and explain the purpose of using excess amine.
markPoints: N-methylethanamide is formed.
One equivalent attacks the acyl chloride.
Excess amine neutralises HCl produced.

rows.requirement: Trace addition–elimination arrow logic in acylation

cards.front: In acylation mechanisms, where should the nucleophile's arrow point?
cards.back: Toward the electrophilic carbonyl carbon.

cards.front: What change restores the carbonyl during the elimination stage?
cards.back: An oxygen lone pair reforms the C=O π bond.

rows.limitation: Many component recall cards exist, but the tested full curved-arrow reaction variety remains limited.

rows.requirement: Compare by-products for acid anhydride versus acyl chloride acylation

cards.front: Which by-product distinguishes acyl chlorides from acid anhydrides?
cards.back: Acyl chlorides give HCl; anhydrides give a carboxylic acid.

rows.requirement: Explain industrial preference for anhydride over chloride in aspirin context

cards.front: Why is ethanoic anhydride preferred industrially over ethanoyl chloride?
cards.back: It avoids producing corrosive hydrogen chloride fumes.

rows.requirement: Use RP10 melting or boiling data to judge purity

cards.front: What can a narrow melting range suggest for an organic solid?
cards.back: Higher purity.

cards.front: Why can a boiling point help assess liquid purity?
cards.back: A pure liquid has a characteristic value at stated pressure.

rows.limitation: Individual precision cards exist, but the topic's mapped exam problems have little original sample-data interpretation.

rows.requirement: Describe planar benzene with equal intermediate-length carbon bonds

cards.front: Why are the six carbon–carbon bonds in benzene equal in length?
cards.back: The π electrons are delocalised across the ring.

rows.requirement: Explain benzene stability through delocalised pi electrons

cards.front: Why is benzene more stable than a hypothetical cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene?
cards.back: Its π electrons are delocalised around the ring, lowering the energy.

questions.prompt: Explain why benzene is more stable than the hypothetical cyclohexatriene with three isolated double bonds.
markPoints: Each carbon has a p orbital; six π electrons are delocalised around the ring.
Delocalisation lowers the energy of the molecule.
Benzene has equal C–C bond lengths and a lower enthalpy of hydrogenation than expected.

rows.requirement: Compare benzene hydrogenation enthalpy with hypothetical isolated double bonds using numbers

cards.front: Why is benzene more stable than a hypothetical cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene?
cards.back: Its π electrons are delocalised around the ring, lowering the energy.

rows.limitation: The main-bank examples explain benzene qualitatively but no directly mapped numerical stability calculation.

rows.requirement: Explain substitution rather than addition and retention of aromaticity

cards.front: Why does benzene favour substitution over addition?
cards.back: Addition would disrupt the stable delocalised π system.

questions.prompt: Why does benzene usually undergo electrophilic substitution instead of addition?
markPoints: Addition would destroy its delocalised aromatic π system.
Substitution restores/preserves aromatic stability after replacement of a hydrogen.

rows.requirement: Recall the electrophile in benzene nitration

cards.front: What is the electrophile in benzene nitration?
cards.back: Nitronium ion, NO₂⁺.

rows.requirement: Explain aromatic electrophilic substitution stages in words

cards.front: What is electrophilic substitution?
cards.back: An electrophile replaces an atom or group, commonly H, on a ring.

questions.prompt: Describe the electrophilic substitution mechanism in nitration of benzene, including restoration of aromaticity.
markPoints: Benzene π electrons attack NO₂⁺ to form a positively charged intermediate.
A proton is lost to reform the delocalised π system.
Product is nitrobenzene.

rows.requirement: Recognise AlCl3 role in Friedel–Crafts acylation

cards.front: What is the role of AlCl₃ in Friedel–Crafts acylation?
cards.back: Lewis acid catalyst for acylium-ion formation.

rows.requirement: Draw electron arrows and intermediates for Friedel–Crafts acylation

cards.front: What catalyst is commonly used for Friedel–Crafts acylation?
cards.back: AlCl₃.

rows.limitation: A catalyst card is not a substitute for drawn mechanism exam practice.

rows.requirement: Identify primary amine from nitrogen atom bonded to one carbon group

cards.front: What is a primary amine?
cards.back: Nitrogen bonded to one carbon-containing group.

rows.requirement: State that ammonia substitution of a halogenoalkane can yield a primary amine

cards.front: What happens after the positively charged RNH₃⁺ intermediate forms?
cards.back: A base removes H⁺, giving a neutral primary amine.

rows.limitation: Year 1 chemistry carries the substitution result, but this is not strongly represented by dedicated A2 amine preparation questions.

rows.requirement: Recognise nitrile reduction as an aminoalkane formation route
rows.limitation: No dedicated short recall evidence identified among the audited amine cards.

rows.requirement: Recall aromatic amine formation from reduction of a nitro group conceptually
rows.limitation: A-level chemistry spec includes the conversion, but topic-specific current cards focus on base strength.

rows.requirement: Explain how aliphatic alkyl substitution increases lone-pair availability

cards.front: Why are primary aliphatic amines often stronger bases than ammonia?
cards.back: Alkyl electron donation increases lone-pair availability.

rows.requirement: Explain why phenylamine is a weaker base than methylamine

cards.front: Why is phenylamine a weaker base than methylamine?
cards.back: Its nitrogen lone pair is partly delocalised into the benzene ring.

questions.prompt: Compare the basicity of phenylamine and methylamine, referring to the nitrogen lone pair.
markPoints: In phenylamine the lone pair is partly delocalised into the benzene ring and less available to accept H⁺.
In methylamine the alkyl group donates electron density, making the lone pair more available.
Methylamine is the stronger base.

rows.requirement: Compare ammonia, primary aliphatic and primary aromatic amines

cards.front: Why are primary aliphatic amines often stronger bases than ammonia?
cards.back: Alkyl electron donation increases lone-pair availability.

cards.front: Why is phenylamine weaker as a base than ammonia?
cards.back: Its nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring.

rows.limitation: Separate comparisons exist; a combined rank/order recall prompt may be helpful if not duplicate.

rows.requirement: Explain nucleophilic role of an amine lone pair

cards.front: Why are amines nucleophiles?
cards.back: The nitrogen lone pair can be donated to an electron-deficient species.

rows.requirement: Identify primary, secondary and tertiary amines from nitrogen bonds

cards.front: How is a secondary amine classified by its nitrogen bonds?
cards.back: Nitrogen is bonded to two carbon-containing groups.

cards.front: How is a tertiary amine classified by its nitrogen bonds?
cards.back: Nitrogen is bonded to three carbon-containing groups.

questions.prompt: Classify (CH₃)₂NH as a primary, secondary or tertiary amine and justify.
markPoints: It is a secondary amine.
The nitrogen is bonded to two carbon-containing groups.

rows.requirement: Recognise quaternary ammonium ions and cationic surfactant use

cards.front: What is a quaternary ammonium ion?
cards.back: A positively charged nitrogen bonded to four carbon groups.

cards.front: What is a use of quaternary ammonium salts?
cards.back: They can act as cationic surfactants.

rows.requirement: Trace repeated alkylation to secondary, tertiary and quaternary products

cards.front: How is a secondary amine classified by its nitrogen bonds?
cards.back: Nitrogen is bonded to two carbon-containing groups.

rows.limitation: A single classification question is not a full unfamiliar reaction-sequence/structure exercise.

rows.requirement: Draw substitution and acylation mechanisms for primary amines

cards.front: What is the common product of a primary amine and an acyl chloride?
cards.back: A secondary amide.

rows.limitation: Product-class recall is strong; arrow-based mechanisms with more than one amine environment remain thin.

rows.requirement: Distinguish condensation and addition polymerisation

cards.front: What happens in condensation polymerisation?
cards.back: Bifunctional monomers join and a small molecule such as H₂O or HCl is eliminated.

rows.requirement: Identify ester links from diol and dicarboxylic acid

cards.front: What links form when a diol reacts with a dicarboxylic acid?
cards.back: Ester links, producing a polyester.

questions.prompt: What type of polymerisation joins a diol to a dicarboxylic acid, and what small molecule is eliminated?
markPoints: Condensation polymerisation.
Ester links form with loss of water.

rows.requirement: Identify amide links from diamine and dicarboxylic acid

cards.front: What links form when a diamine reacts with a dicarboxylic acid?
cards.back: Amide links, producing a polyamide.

questions.prompt: A polyamide chain is formed by reacting diamine with dicarboxylic acid. Identify the linking functional group.
markPoints: The repeating link is –CONH– (amide link).
Water is eliminated during condensation formation.

rows.requirement: Identify amino acid polymerisation with peptide links

cards.front: What is a peptide bond?
cards.back: The amide link, −CONH−, formed between amino acids by condensation.

rows.requirement: Draw a complete polyester repeat unit from two monomer structures

cards.front: What bond links monomers in a polyester?
cards.back: Ester linkage, –COO–.

rows.limitation: No concrete unseen polymer repeat-unit drawing problem mapped in the main bank.

rows.requirement: Recover monomer structures from a polyamide chain fragment

cards.front: What bond links monomers in a polyamide?
cards.back: Amide linkage, –CONH–.

rows.limitation: No concrete reverse-polymer drawing problem mapped.

rows.requirement: Compare typical uses of Terylene, nylon 6,6 and Kevlar
rows.limitation: General polymer cards do not directly recall uses of these named polymers.

rows.requirement: Explain hydrogen bonding between polyamide chains

cards.front: What links form when a diamine reacts with a dicarboxylic acid?
cards.back: Amide links, producing a polyamide.

rows.limitation: Amide-link formation is recalled, but the intermolecular force explanation is not directly evidenced.

rows.requirement: Explain why polyesters and polyamides can undergo hydrolysis

cards.front: Why can polyesters be hydrolysed?
cards.back: Their polymer chains contain ester links.

cards.front: Why can polyamides be hydrolysed?
cards.back: Their polymer chains contain amide links.

questions.prompt: Explain why a polyester can undergo hydrolysis whereas poly(ethene) is highly resistant.
markPoints: A polyester has hydrolysable ester links in the backbone.
Poly(ethene) has a carbon–carbon backbone without hydrolysable functional groups.

rows.requirement: Explain why saturated polyalkenes resist hydrolysis

cards.front: Why are polyalkenes generally resistant to hydrolysis?
cards.back: Their backbones contain C–C bonds, not hydrolysable ester or amide links.

rows.requirement: Discuss incineration versus recycling trade-offs

cards.front: Why can incinerating polymer waste cause environmental problems?
cards.back: It releases CO₂ and may produce harmful gases if emissions are not controlled.

cards.front: Why can recycling mixed polymer waste be difficult?
cards.back: Different polymers have different properties and may need sorting before reprocessing.

questions.prompt: Explain a benefit and a drawback of incinerating plastic waste for energy recovery.
markPoints: Benefit: waste volume decreases and energy can be recovered.
Drawbacks include CO₂ emissions and potentially harmful gases depending on polymer and controls.

rows.requirement: State meaning of zwitterion and dual acid/base properties

cards.front: Define a zwitterion.
cards.back: An ion with both positive and negative charges but no overall charge.

questions.prompt: Explain why amino acids can behave as both acids and bases.
markPoints: Carboxyl group can donate H⁺.
Amino group can accept H⁺.
They are amphoteric.

rows.requirement: Explain amino acid predominant ionic form in acid versus alkali

cards.front: What form does a simple amino acid predominantly take in strongly acidic solution?
cards.back: A positive ion with –NH₃⁺ and –COOH groups.

cards.front: What form does a simple amino acid predominantly take in strongly alkaline solution?
cards.back: A negative ion with –NH₂ and –COO⁻ groups.

rows.requirement: Draw unfamiliar amino acid as zwitterion and acid/alkali forms

cards.front: What is a zwitterion?
cards.back: A molecule containing both positive and negative charges but with no overall charge.

questions.prompt: Describe the zwitterion structure of glycine in water around neutral pH.
markPoints: The amino group is protonated to –NH₃⁺.
The carboxyl group is deprotonated to –COO⁻.
Overall molecule carries equal positive and negative charges.

rows.limitation: Only a simple glycine example is mapped; unfamiliar multi-form drawings need scrutiny.

rows.requirement: Define peptide bond and state hydrolysis outcome

cards.front: What is a peptide bond?
cards.back: The amide link, −CONH−, formed between amino acids by condensation.

cards.front: What is produced when all the peptide bonds in a protein are hydrolysed?
cards.back: Its constituent amino acids.

rows.requirement: Distinguish protein primary, secondary and tertiary structure

cards.front: What is the primary structure of a protein?
cards.back: Its amino-acid sequence.

cards.front: What are two common protein secondary structures?
cards.back: Alpha helices and beta pleated sheets.

cards.front: What is a protein's tertiary structure?
cards.back: Its overall three-dimensional folding.

rows.requirement: Recall hydrogen bonding and sulfur–sulfur stabilisation

cards.front: What interactions stabilise protein secondary structure?
cards.back: Hydrogen bonds.

cards.front: What covalent link can stabilise a protein's tertiary structure?
cards.back: Disulfide bridge, –S–S–.

questions.prompt: What interactions help stabilise the tertiary structure of a protein?
markPoints: Hydrogen bonding between suitable groups.
Disulfide links between cysteine residues can stabilise structure.
Additional ionic and other intermolecular interactions may contribute.

rows.requirement: Identify amino acids by TLC Rf and locating agents

cards.front: What locates amino-acid spots on some chromatograms?
cards.back: Ninhydrin.

questions.prompt: A TLC spot travels 3.2 cm and the solvent front 8.0 cm from the baseline. Calculate Rf.
markPoints: Rf=distance moved by spot/distance moved by solvent front.

rows.limitation: A general Rf calculation exists; identification from multiple supplied standards and ninhydrin observations not mapped.

rows.requirement: Draw dipeptide and tripeptide structures from supplied amino acids

cards.front: What group links neighbouring amino acids in a polypeptide?
cards.back: Peptide (amide) link, –CONH–.

rows.limitation: No mapped three-amino-acid structure drawing task.

rows.requirement: Identify protein secondary/tertiary structure from labelled diagrams

cards.front: What are two common protein secondary structures?
cards.back: Alpha helices and beta pleated sheets.

cards.front: What is a protein's tertiary structure?
cards.back: Its overall three-dimensional folding.

rows.limitation: No mapped novel protein-structure diagram problem.

rows.requirement: Explain stereospecificity of enzyme active sites

cards.front: Why can enzymes be stereospecific?
cards.back: The active-site shape can favour only one enantiomer.

rows.requirement: Explain inhibition by an active-site blocking molecule

cards.front: What is an enzyme inhibitor?
cards.back: A substance that reduces the enzyme's catalytic action.

rows.requirement: Apply stereospecificity to one of two enantiomers binding in a hypothetical active site

cards.front: Why can enzymes be stereospecific?
cards.back: The active-site shape can favour only one enantiomer.

rows.requirement: Identify phosphate, deoxyribose and a base as nucleotide constituents

cards.front: What is a nucleotide made of in DNA?
cards.back: Phosphate, 2-deoxyribose and a base.

questions.prompt: Describe a nucleotide's three components in DNA.
markPoints: A phosphate group.
A deoxyribose sugar.
One nitrogen-containing base (A, T, G or C).

questions.prompt: State the complementary DNA bases pairing with adenine and cytosine.
markPoints: Adenine pairs with thymine.
Cytosine pairs with guanine.

questions.prompt: Explain which bonds connect nucleotides in one DNA strand and which interactions link opposite strands.

Hydrogen bonds form between complementary bases on opposite strands.

cards.front: How many hydrogen bonds link cytosine and guanine in DNA?

cards.front: What does a ¹³C NMR peak correspond to?
cards.back: One distinct carbon environment.

cards.front: What does the number of signals in a carbon-13 NMR spectrum indicate?
cards.back: Number of different carbon environments.

rows.requirement: Explain chemical shift and reference chemical environments

cards.front: What does chemical shift tell you?
cards.back: It indicates the electronic environment around a nucleus relative to TMS.

cards.front: What does 'chemical shift' describe?
cards.back: Peak position relative to a reference signal, in ppm.

rows.requirement: Recall TMS reference and chemical shift zero

cards.front: Why is TMS used as an NMR reference?
cards.back: It gives one sharp signal at δ = 0 and is chemically inert/volatile.

cards.front: Why is TMS assigned chemical shift zero?
cards.back: It is the reference standard.

rows.requirement: Recall deuterated solvents' purpose in proton NMR

cards.front: What does a deuterated solvent reduce in proton NMR?
cards.back: Unwanted solvent ¹H signals.

rows.requirement: Use 1H NMR integration to identify relative proton counts

cards.front: What does integration in a ¹H NMR spectrum show?
cards.back: The relative number of protons in each environment.

questions.prompt: A proton spectrum contains integrations in ratio 3:2:1. State what this tells you and one limitation of integration alone.
markPoints: The signals represent three, two and one equivalent proton groups in relative proportion.
Integration alone does not identify which functional groups or connectivity are present.

rows.requirement: Apply n+1 rule to doublets, triplets and quartets

cards.front: What splitting pattern does one adjacent equivalent proton cause?
cards.back: Doublet.

cards.front: What splitting pattern do two adjacent equivalent protons cause?
cards.back: Triplet.

questions.prompt: A ¹H NMR signal appears as a triplet. Assuming usual n+1 splitting, how many equivalent neighbouring hydrogens cause it?
markPoints: Thus n=2 neighbouring equivalent hydrogens.

rows.requirement: Use NMR chemical shift, splitting and integration together for structure inference

cards.front: What does the number of ¹H NMR signals show?
cards.back: Number of distinct proton environments.

questions.prompt: A compound has formula C₄H₈O₂ and three distinct proton NMR signals: δ 1.2 ppm (triplet, integration 3), δ 2.3 ppm (quartet, integration 2), and δ 3.7 ppm (singlet, integration 3). Suggest an ester structure, explain the splitting and integration of each signal, and justify why the total signal integration fits the molecular formula.
markPoints: The proposed ester is methyl propanoate CH₃CH₂COOCH₃.
Triplet at ~1.2 ppm integrates to 3H for CH₃ adjacent to CH₂.
Quartet at ~2.3 ppm integrates to 2H for CH₂ adjacent to CH₃ and carbonyl.
Singlet at ~3.7 ppm integrates to 3H for OCH₃ with no neighbouring proton on the adjacent oxygen.
The n+1 rule explains triplet from 2 neighbours and quartet from 3 neighbours.
Integrated protons total 3 + 2 + 3 = 8, matching C₄H₈O₂.
The chemical shifts are consistent with alkyl group next to C=O and methoxy ester oxygen.

rows.requirement: Use C-13 plus H-1 data with booklet to distinguish multiple possible structures

cards.front: What does a ¹³C NMR peak correspond to?
cards.back: One distinct carbon environment.

rows.requirement: Flag that n+1 AQA required cases are limited to doublet, triplet and quartet

cards.front: What does the n+1 rule describe in simple ¹H NMR spectra?
cards.back: A proton environment with n equivalent neighbouring protons is split into n+1 peaks.

questions.prompt: A hydrogen has 5 equivalent neighbouring protons. Using the simple n+1 rule, how many lines are predicted in its ¹H NMR signal?
markPoints: For simple first-order splitting, multiplicity=n+1.
Predicted lines=6.

rows.limitation: A generated question about five neighbouring protons goes beyond the named required splitting patterns; keep as enrichment, not compulsory core.

rows.requirement: Define stationary and mobile phases in chromatography

cards.front: What does the mobile phase do in chromatography?
cards.back: It carries the components through the stationary phase.

cards.front: What is the stationary phase?
cards.back: The phase with which sample components interact while separating.

rows.requirement: Identify TLC stationary solid and solvent mobile phase

cards.front: What is the stationary phase in TLC typically?
cards.back: A solid adsorbent such as silica.

cards.front: What is the mobile phase in TLC?
cards.back: A solvent moving up the plate.

rows.requirement: Recognise column chromatography uses packed solid and moving solvent

cards.front: What is the mobile phase in column chromatography?
cards.back: A liquid solvent.

rows.requirement: Identify GC carrier gas, stationary phase and retention time

cards.front: What is the mobile phase in gas chromatography?
cards.back: A carrier gas.

cards.front: What can form the stationary phase in gas chromatography?
cards.back: A solid or a non-volatile liquid coating a solid.

cards.front: Define retention time in gas chromatography.
cards.back: The time between sample injection and detection of a component.

rows.requirement: Explain relative solubility and adsorption/retention separation

cards.front: Why can chromatography separate mixture components?
cards.back: They distribute differently between stationary and mobile phases.

cards.front: How does a higher affinity for the stationary phase affect travel?
cards.back: The component travels more slowly.

rows.requirement: Calculate Rf from chromatogram distances

cards.front: What is Rf in thin-layer chromatography?
cards.back: distance moved by solute ÷ distance moved by solvent front.

questions.prompt: A TLC spot travels 3.2 cm and the solvent front 8.0 cm from the baseline. Calculate Rf.
markPoints: Rf=distance moved by spot/distance moved by solvent front.

rows.requirement: Compare Rf values and retention times against standards

cards.front: Why compare Rf values under identical conditions?
cards.back: Rf changes with solvent and stationary phase.

cards.front: What does a retention time help identify in gas chromatography?
cards.back: A component, when compared under the same conditions.

rows.limitation: Numerical Rf drills exist but an unfamiliar multiple-standards interpretation with uncertainty is not mapped.

rows.requirement: Explain why GC coupled with mass spec improves identification

cards.front: Why may gas chromatography be coupled with mass spectrometry?
cards.back: To separate components and help identify them by mass spectra.

rows.requirement: Interpret a full RP12 TLC data table including unknown mixture

cards.front: What does a mixture giving several TLC spots suggest?
cards.back: It contains several components.

rows.limitation: Existing practice emphasizes one-spot Rf arithmetic, not a multi-sample chromatogram data interpretation.
